newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK HORSERACING GAMBLERS GRAB WORLD RECORD PAYOUT.
newsitem.headline: HK HORSERACING GAMBLERS GRAB WORLD RECORD PAYOUT.

text.p: A gambling bonanza that gripped Hong Kong ended on Sunday with a world record HK$719 million (US$92 million) payout that concluded a horseracing season two weeks before the colony reverts to Chinese rule.
Punters had to identify the first three horses in three races for a Triple Trio wager that excited gambling-mad Hong Kong which annually has a horserace betting turnover equal to about US$10 billion.
Nobody got all nine horses, but 353.5 bets of $HK10 each collected $HK2.03 million.
The "Guinness Book of World Records" lists the last world horse-racing payout record as US$1.627 million in California in 1987.
About 88,000 people, many first-time horse gamblers, crammed into the Hong Kong Jockey Club's Sha Tin race course to test their luck.
The club distributes profits to community causes and says it is one of the world's five largest philanthropic organisations.
The Triple Trio payout had been widely expected to burst through records with a carried-over HK$198 million jackpot.

In the end no one, among the one million Hong Kong people who regularly gamble on horses, got the positions right, and "consolation prizes" of HK$2.03 million each went out to the successful HK$10 wagers.
The Club has said it would distribute the payout to those who correctly guessed the first two legs if no one wins a straight triple.
To win the Triple Trio, punters had to choose the first three horses across the line in any order in three selected races, a wager with more than 48 million possibilities.
The races were the last before British-ruled Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30, ending 156 years of colonialism. A new season begins later in the year.

The Jockey Club, founded in 1884 and holding a monopoly on gambling in the British colony, received in weekend bets on the Triple Trio a staggering HK$675.7 million - equal to about 100 dollars for each of the 6.4 million population.
"This is best outcome as many people won which discouraged syndicated betting," Mimi Cunningham, a manager at the club, said.

Anti-graft police, probing an alleged race-fixing scandal, stormed the Sha Tin racecourse last March and hauled away 39 people, including jockeys and trainers, for questioning. Six appeared in court on Friday accused of illegal bets with bookmakers.
The track is one of the biggest businesses in the territory and its multi-billion dollar turnover outperforms some blue-chip stocks like Nike and Microsoft, the club said in a statement.

"I do not like the media for portraying Hong Kong as a casino detached from the actual races...we pay a lot of attention to bringing up the standards of horses and rules," said Alan Li, a club stewart. (US$1=HK$7.8)
